source: McKinsey & Company, Postmerger Management Practice (2002) — client survey and case studies, as reproduced in Aswath Damodaran's acquisitions lecture packet (valpacket3, p.116-117). Attrition range and error lists from the same slides.
refresh: This is a published academic reference, not a market data series, so it does not go stale the way spreads do. Replace it if a larger or more recent post-merger realization study becomes available, and record which study a deal analysis used. Damodaran's current packets: https://pages.stern.nyu.edu/~adamodar/
headline: 70% of mergers failed to achieve the revenue synergies expected at announcement; a large majority delivered 90% or more of expected cost savings.

revenue.basis: Midpoint of the 61-70% band, which is where the cumulative revenue-synergy distribution crosses 50% of mergers.
revenue.attrition_basis: Midpoint of the 2%-5% integration customer-loss range reported on the same slides. Applies to revenue synergies only.

cost.basis: Midpoint of the 91-100% band, where the cumulative cost-saving distribution crosses 50% of mergers.
cost.attrition_basis: Integration customer loss does not reduce a cost saving; it reduces the revenue it was meant to support.

revenue: Ignoring or underestimating customer losses from integration, typically 2%-5%.
Growth and share targets out of line with market growth and competitive response — no outside view.
cost: Underestimating the one-time costs to achieve the savings.
Not sanity-checking management estimates against precedent transactions.
No bottom-up analysis such as a location-by-location overlap review.

odds_findings: Cost synergies are far more likely to be delivered than growth synergies.
Concrete synergies planned before the merger closes beat fuzzy ones.
Synergy shows up much more often when a named person is accountable for delivering it.
A sole bidder keeps more of the synergy than one of several bidders.
